💡 Key Takeaways
  • From first endpoint to global fleet: 14 more releases for managed endpoints and HyperPod Inference.
  • According to recent reports, in September, Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review covered 13 launches that shortened the path from a model to a production endpoint.
  • It has been revealed that once a model is in production, the questions change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From first endpoint to global fleet: 14 more releases for managed endpoints and HyperPod Inference.

According to recent reports, in September, Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review covered 13 launches that shortened the path from a model to a production endpoint. Most of them answered one question: how do I get this model serving quickly and reliably? This post covers the 14 launches that came next, bringing the total for 2026 to 27.

It has been revealed that once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them.

Recent findings suggest that for HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway and the Global Inference Gateway deliver the routing and multi-Region work, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts.

According to recent reports, to keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they debuted a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the releases from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat.

Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the rolls out in each.

The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console.

Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A newly introduced agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents.

Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI.

Recent findings suggest that the April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs, then Inference optimization. Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model.

SageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio.

Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK.

Industry observers note that benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration to a real-time endpoint in a single call.

Recent findings suggest that the SDK also supports longer workflows. You can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM, and you can resume from a completed job so that deployment happens in a different notebook or pipeline stage without re-running the benchmarks.

Developer guide: Get recommendations for models with LoRA adapters.

Many teams use LoRA adapters to specialize one foundation model for several use cases. Each adapter kept in GPU memory reduces the number of concurrent requests the endpoint can serve, and the right balance depends on the instance type, the number of adapters, and the traffic profile.

Inference recommendations now accept adapters as Model Package Amazon Resource Names (ARNs), for adapters produced by SageMaker fine-tuning, or as S3 URIs, for adapters from external pipelines such as Hugging Face PEFT. SageMaker AI benchmarks combinations of adapter count and concurrency on real GPU infrastructure and returns ranked results for your workload. The output lists both formats for every adapter. The recommended deployment uses SageMaker Inference Components, with one component for the base model and one for each adapter, so you can add, enhancement, or remove an adapter without disrupting the base model or the other adapters.

Blog: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI.

In a recent development, right-sizing an endpoint means finding the highest concurrency it can sustain without breaching latency or error targets. Until now, that meant picking concurrency levels by hand, running a sweep, checking the results against the service level agreement (SLA), and repeating with a narrower range whenever the model or instance changed.

Inference recommendations now include a search that finds that boundary directly. Set search_recipe to max-concurrency-under-sla and supply targets for any combination of maximum TTFT, maximum time per output token, maximum end-to-end latency, and maximum error rate. The benchmarking engine (AIPerf) starts from a broad range, narrows it based on which probes pass or fail, and converges in fewer iterations than a linear sweep. The result reports the largest passing concurrency (feasible_max) or, if no level qualifies, the smallest failing one (infeasible_min).

The search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. Optional parameters (concurrency_min, concurrency_max, search_max_iterations, and search_initial_points) bound the cost and speed up convergence.

Blog: New agent skill: Amazon SageMaker optimized generative AI inference for your coding agent.

Engineers increasingly ask their coding agent which instance and container to use. Without grounded knowledge and access to real benchmarks, the agent can only guess, and a wrong instance choice demonstrates up later as missed latency targets or wasted spend.

The aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. Engineers describe what they need in plain language, and the agent can do the following:.

Answers are grounded in measured performance and delivered as SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that engineers review and run under their own credentials. Setup takes about 10 minutes. The skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces.

Recent findings suggest that for the support team, one recommendation job that includes all four adapters, followed by a concurrency search against the 500 millisecond TTFT target, replaces the manual sweeps they ran in April. The engineer who owns it can start the job from a notebook or ask a coding agent to run it.

In a recent development, the support assistant does not run alone. An embedding model, a reranker, and a small classifier that routes tickets live in the same account, and each uses a fraction of a GPU. On a standard endpoint, each model copy still held a whole accelerator, so the team ran out of placement slots while GPU memory sat unused.

Developer guide: Inference Components in the SageMaker AI Console.

With Inference Components, you can host several models on one endpoint and size and scale each model separately. Until now, they were available only through the SDK and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Every create, resize, and scaling policy had to be scripted, and there was no single view of what each model was using.

In the SageMaker AI console, you can now create, view, enhancement, and delete inference components:.

The console calls the same SageMaker AI APIs as the SDK and CLI, so teams can start on the console and automate later, or manage scripted components visually.

Blog: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints.

GPU partitioning uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology to divide one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions, depending on the accelerator. Each partition has dedicated GPU compute and memory, with complete hardware isolation. You define the partition layout when you create an endpoint for inference components and choose a partition type for each component. Applications keep invoking models by inference component name, so client code does not change.

MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. You pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance, not from a lower hourly price.

Figure 2: Three small models on three GPUs, compared with the same models in partitions of one GPU.

For the support team, the embedding model, the reranker, and the classifier now run in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint, and the team manages every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console.

The team’s next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance. They have also noticed that long, retrieval-heavy prompts slow token generation for every other user on the endpoint. For a model this size, they move the workload to HyperPod Inference, which gives them dedicated clusters and Kubernetes-native control. The support assistant stays on managed endpoints.

Blog: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference.

Part 1 covered two building blocks for large models on HyperPod: disaggregated prefill and decode in Inference Operator v3.2, and KV-aware routing as part of the managed tiered KV cache. This launch adds multi-node serving and changes who operates the stack. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source inference framework that provides multi-node sharded serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. Teams could already run Dynamo on their own Kubernetes clusters, but they had to build and operate everything around it: placing all the nodes of a replica together, wiring Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking so prefill can hand its KV cache to decode at hardware speed, maintaining serving images, and recovering when one failed node takes down a multi-node replica.

In a recent development, with this launch, Dynamo runs as a managed serving engine on HyperPod. Dynamo makes the serving decisions: how the model is sharded, how prefill and decode are split, and where each request goes. HyperPod provides what those decisions depend on:.

The capabilities Dynamo brings to HyperPod are:.

There are three ways to start. Teams running Dynamo on self-managed Kubernetes can bring their existing DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) manifests largely unchanged. Teams already on HyperPod Inference can revision the add-on and add a short dynamoSpec block to an existing InferenceEndpointConfig, which HyperPod converts into a DGD, while existing endpoints keep serving. Teams new to both can create a cluster with the add-on and Dynamo enabled from the console. In each case, clients call a standard OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so client code does not change.

Managed Dynamo supports vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, and is available in the Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Figure 3: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference.

Recent findings suggest that for the support team, the reasoning model runs as one sharded replica across several nodes, with separate prefill and decode pools. When a node fails, HyperPod replaces it and reschedules the replica without a page to the on-call engineer.

The support assistant now serves customers in North America and Europe, so the team runs endpoints and HyperPod clusters in two Regions. During the US morning peak, requests queue in the US Region while GPUs the team already pays for sit idle in Europe. Some European traffic must also stay in Europe.

Routing decides whether capacity a team owns does useful work. It happens at four levels, and the releases below cover one level each: which instance serves a request inside an endpoint, which pod inside a HyperPod cluster, which cluster across a fleet, and which Regional endpoint across Regions and accounts.

Figure 4: Routing across Regions and inside each endpoint or cluster, on both deployment paths.

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing.

Applications with long prompts or multi-turn conversations repeat a large prefix across requests. A model server can reuse the matching KV cache, but only if the next request reaches the instance that holds it. Prefix-aware routing, covered in part 1, fingerprints the start of each prompt and sends matching prompts to the same instance. Because it works from request history, its view of each instance’s cache becomes less accurate as the model server adds and evicts entries.

KV-cache-aware routing uses the cache state the model container reports. The container publishes cache creation and eviction events to a central cache index, and SageMaker AI routes each request to an eligible instance that holds the longest matching cached prefix. This raises cache reuse for long-context prompts, multi-turn conversations, and workloads that share dynamic prompt prefixes.

Industry observers note that it works with single-model endpoints and endpoints that use inference components, including LoRA adapters. It supports InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, and the OpenAI-compatible API for Completions and Chat Completions payloads. You turn it on in the endpoint configuration. The first release requires an AWS-verified model container that implements the cache-event, tokenization, metrics, and OpenAI-compatible interfaces. You can track KV cache hit rate in detailed inference observability.

Which one to use. Prefix-aware routing works with any container and needs no container changes. KV-cache-aware routing needs a verified container and tracks the actual cache, which helps most when prefixes vary or caches turn over quickly.

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway.

According to recent reports, inside a HyperPod cluster, capacity and demand rarely line up. One pod can be partway through a long-context request with its KV cache nearly full, while the next pod sits idle or already holds the prompt prefix or LoRA adapter the next request needs. Without visibility into that GPU state, latest requests queue behind busy pods, and teams add GPUs to protect latency instead of using the ones they have. Each model also had its own endpoint, so clients had to track one endpoint per model.

The Inference Gateway is a GPU-aware router that installs with the HyperPod Inference Operator add-on and gives each cluster one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for all of its models. For each request, it reads live signals from every model pod and picks the best one, with weights you can tune per workload:.

Compared with round-robin routing, it reduced P99 TTFT by up to 97% on mixed GPU generations and by up to 98% under bursty traffic. It is available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Blog: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway.

The Inference Gateway routes within a cluster, and each cluster can serve only the requests sent to it. A request can wait on a saturated cluster in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another. Clients had to choose a cluster themselves, and when a cluster failed, an engineer had to move traffic by hand.

The Global Inference Gateway gives teams one SageMaker-managed endpoint across every cluster they register. For each request, it scores clusters on queue depth, free KV cache, proximity to the caller, and recent error rate, and sends the request to the best one over the AWS private backbone. The Inference Gateway in that cluster still picks the pod. Requests authenticate with SigV4 and IAM. When a cluster becomes saturated or unhealthy, traffic shifts to the next-best cluster in under 30 seconds with no action from the client, and the cluster rejoins the pool when it recovers. Routing weights are tunable, with defaults if you leave them unset.

Recent findings suggest that adding or removing a model or cluster does not change anything for the applications that call the endpoint. No cluster is reachable until you publish it, and the published resources stay in your account. The Global Inference Gateway is available in the Regions listed in the AWS documentation.

Blog: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.

On managed endpoints, the same idea takes the form of the Cross-Region Inference Routing, managed routing that sends real-time and asynchronous requests across Regional endpoints a team has already deployed, in the same account or in different accounts. You group endpoints that serve the same model under a routing target, and the application invokes the target instead of a specific Regional endpoint. The router does not add capacity, replicate models, or deploy endpoints, and the existing invocation path keeps working.

The router replaces the failover logic teams build themselves today:.

Figure 5: Cross-Region Inference Router request flow.

The two cross-Region launches apply the same idea on each deployment path. The team keeps ownership of its clusters and endpoints, and SageMaker supplies the routing, the private connectivity, and the failover.

For the support team, the US morning peak now overflows to capacity in Europe on both paths, and requests that must stay in Europe are restricted to European Regions in the router policy.

In a recent development, two months after the move, the team adds retrieval to the support assistant, and the average prompt length roughly doubles. TTFT is now higher than it was at launch, but nothing has failed, so every alarm stays green. When the team finds a better configuration, they will need to roll it out on large GPU instances that are hard to get more of.

Blog: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints.

Recent findings suggest that amazon SageMaker AI now continuously monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. When a finding clears its confidence threshold, a notification appears on the AWS Management Console, and the same message arrives by email for teams that work in notebooks and the CLI. The recommended action opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker AI Studio with the finding already filled in, so the analysis, the comparison, and the deployment change happen in one conversation. Nothing deploys until you apply it, and you can turn monitoring off at any time.

There are three types of findings:.

In a recent development, A standard rolling update replaces an endpoint one batch at a time, and every batch runs on newly provisioned instances. On a large GPU fleet, that means finding newly introduced capacity at every step, and an update can fail partway through when the next batch of instances is not available. Each released instance must also finish cleanup before it can be used again, which slows the rollout.

Sources indicate that sageMaker AI now updates models in place. It provisions one small batch of additional instances at the start, shifts traffic to that batch, and then updates the instances it frees, reusing them to roll the change across the rest of the fleet. The update still rolls out in stages, but it needs latest capacity only once. For a fleet of 20 instances with a batch size of 2, the update acquires 2 new instances instead of 20. Customers do not need to change anything. As with container caching in part 1, the improvement applies automatically to rolling model updates.

Sources indicate that figure 6: A rolling upgrade acquires fresh instances at every step. An in-place rolling update acquires one batch at the start and reuses the rest of the fleet.

According to recent reports, for the support team, a Drift Watch finding quantifies the TTFT regression and opens a upcoming recommendation job against recent traffic. They roll out the updated model with one batch of extra instances, instead of finding new GPU capacity for every instance in the fleet.

The numbering continues from the 13 launches in part 1.

Sources indicate that 14. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026). A guided, low-code workflow for ranked, benchmarked configurations, with deployment from Studio.

Recent findings suggest that 15. Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026). Benchmark, recommend, and deploy from a notebook or pipeline, with parallel and resumable jobs.

Sources indicate that 16. LoRA adapter support in inference recommendations (September 2026). Benchmarks adapter count against concurrency and deploys adapters as inference components.

Recent findings suggest that 17. SLA-based concurrency search (September 2026). Finds the highest concurrency that meets TTFT, latency, and error-rate targets.

Sources indicate that 18. Agent skill for optimized generative AI inference (October 2026). Instance selection, benchmarking, and run comparison from MCP-compatible coding agents.

Industry observers note that 19. Inference Components in the SageMaker AI console (October 2026). Create, scale, and monitor each model on a multi-model endpoint without scripts.

According to recent reports, 20. GPU partitioning with NVIDIA MIG (October 2026). Up to seven isolated partitions per GPU, assigned per inference component.

According to recent reports, 21. Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference (November 2026). Multi-node and disaggregated serving, with HyperPod operating the platform underneath.

Industry observers note that 22. KV-cache-aware routing (November 2026). Routes each request to the instance that holds the longest cached prefix, based on cache events from the container.

It has been revealed that 23. Inference Gateway for HyperPod (September 2026). One endpoint per cluster with GPU-aware routing, and up to 97% lower P99 TTFT than round-robin.

Sources indicate that 24. Global Inference Gateway for HyperPod (November 2026). One endpoint across clusters and Regions, with failover in under 2 minutes.

In a recent development, 25. Cross-Region Inference Router. Routes across Regional and cross-account endpoints over PrivateLink, with overflow and residency guardrails.

26. Continuous performance monitoring. Detects latency drift, configuration gaps, and idle capacity, with a guided fix in SageMaker AI Studio.

27. In-place rolling model updates (November 2026). Rolls out model updates with one batch of additional instances at the start, then reuses existing instances across the fleet.

By the end of the year, the support team serves four product lines from one base model, runs its small models on shared GPUs, serves a reasoning model that no single instance can hold, and routes traffic across two Regions with residency controls. It did not need to build its own benchmarking harness, failover logic, or drift monitoring to get there.

In a recent development, part 1 argued that advantage in AI inference comes from operating an efficient inference stack. These 14 launches apply that argument to the months after launch day. The AWS Experience-Based Acceleration program can help your team put them to work by benchmarking your workloads and configuring your inference stack against your SLAs and cost targets.

On managed endpoints, we proposal to extend in-place rolling updates in early 2027 with scale-in-first updates, which remove the need for any additional instances during a model update.

According to recent reports, documentation and getting-started guides for every capability in this post are in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Start with the section that matches your current problem. If your traffic has changed since you deployed, re-run inference recommendations. If you are short on placement slots, move small models onto partitioned GPUs. If requests queue while capacity you own sits idle, register your clusters and endpoints for cross-Region routing.

Sources indicate that view CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to patch to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released newly introduced versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Automation Software Products are affected:.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

#7980. Tech Report: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Fresh Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2083 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Fresh Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • According to recent reports, every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

According to recent reports, every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Industry observers note that foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to upcoming series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

Industry observers note that businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Industry observers note that figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Industry observers note that figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

Sources indicate that -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

Recent findings suggest that -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

It has been revealed that figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

Sources indicate that to get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

It has been revealed that when the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

According to recent reports, the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Sources indicate that figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

In a recent development, AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each newly introduced reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

It has been revealed that figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as newly introduced sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

Recent findings suggest that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Industry observers note that figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

In a recent development, fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

Sources indicate that A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

Sources indicate that the bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

Recent findings suggest that an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

According to recent reports, on each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A newly introduced cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Sources indicate that banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

View CSAF Summary The products listed below contain an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow an on-path attacker to take over the session of a legitimate user and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the victim user. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC are affected: SIMATIC BATCH V9.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Information Server 2020 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Information Server 2022 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC PCS 7 V9.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Process Historian 2020 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Process Historian 2022 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V17 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V18 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V19 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V20 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V21 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V7.5 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V8.0 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V8.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens SIMATIC BATCH V9.1 1 Vulnerability Weak Authentication Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-58114 Affected systems do not properly secure their remote user authentication with the deprecated NTLM protocol. This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers, who have achieved a machine in the middle position, to relay NTLM authentication and impersonate a legitimate user. The potential impact depends on the services that are accessible, e.g. a SQL server used by WinCC. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends customers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. #7976. Latest Update: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1225 w)

Latest Update: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency.
  • This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS.
  • The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks.

This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer.

The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything:.

These flows, from estimating benefits to setup, require the following:.

Industry observers note that we gave the agent this prompt: “My vLLM fleet serves a legal assistant with 64K-token contexts on p5 instances. Returning conversations take 13 seconds for the first token because the GPU recomputes the full conversation history every turn. How do I fix this?”.

Recent findings suggest that the agent matches the request to the skill and, in Kiro, asks for approval before loading it. The answer identifies that the latency was caused by cold prefill, and three things in the answer matter for a real deployment. First, it checks for fixes that need no latest infrastructure. If you turned off prefix caching, turning it back on can speed up back-to-back turns. If the GPU prefix cache hit rate is already above 90% with session affinity, you might not need a shared KV cache. Second, it identifies constraints specific to the legal AI assistant. A shared KV cache can let one tenant tell from response times whether another tenant sent the same text. Cases that must stay isolated get separate caches, and tenants that share a cache add their own ID to the KV hash. Third, it doesn’t guess the size. It asks for the model and TP size, KV data type, replica count and routing, and how long customers wait between turns.

Figure 1: The diagnosis and proposed architecture for the legal assistant.

To size the savings, we gave the agent an example fleet of 8 p5 instances that serve 64,000-token prompts for a multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant. The agent looked up the GPU and cache node prices and derived the prefill rate and KV size from benchmarks. Finally, the agent recommended two cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes for distributed KV caching. The following figure highlights the agent’s summary and the inputs it used.

Figure 2: The agent’s summary and inputs. It looked up both prices in the AWS price list and explains how it arrived at the recompute figure.

We didn’t provide a cache hit rate, which is the share of recomputed tokens the cache would serve. The agent therefore presents scenarios and recommends a KVTrace run to identify the cache hit rate. KVTrace records the KV cache events from vLLM or SGLang. It then replays them offline against a shared KV cache of each candidate size. The recorder never writes token IDs or prompt text. Traces hold block hashes and token counts. Block hashes come from token content, so pass --anonymize-key-file when your prompts are sensitive. The skill records on every GPU server for a representative window, such as a full business day. The agent also notes that freed GPU time turns into dollars only if you run fewer servers or serve more traffic on the same ones.

Figure 3: The top of a KVTrace report from synthetic demo traffic. It recommends the smallest capacity that reaches 90% of the savings ceiling.

We prompted the agent with: “Set up a shared L2 KV cache for LLM inference, starting from scratch.” Before it creates anything, the agent requests your confirmation to set up the suggested cache node count in your Availability Zone, at the estimated price. Once confirmed, it creates the right security group with EFA permissions, and a Valkey 9.1 cluster that uses a custom parameter group with caching eviction policies. LMCache gets its own cache user, with the password in AWS Secrets Manager. The agent prepares the GPU servers and starts one LMCache server per GPU server. Then it checks the cluster with a small test object and confirms that repeated prompts load their KV state from the cache over Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). On a GPU fleet, the skill checks the measured L2 share against the KVTrace prediction. For the full setup with every command, see Getting started with distributed KV caching in the Amazon ElastiCache documentation.

In a recent development, prompt: “My LMCache server connects to the ElastiCache cluster and BLOB.RDMA_HELLO succeeds, but actual data transfers are failing. INFO largeobj indicates rdma_write_errors climbing. What’s wrong?”.

In a recent development, following the skill’s troubleshooting guide, the agent reasons from the symptom pattern and identifies the likely cause as a security group that blocks EFA traffic between its own members. It provides you commands to check and fix the rule.

Figure 4: The agent explains the symptom, then gives commands to check and fix the security group.

In a recent development, you can get the distributed KV caching skill or the AWS MCP Server from the Agent Toolkit for AWS. Then describe your problem or ask your AI agent to cut costs and latency on your GPU fleet to get started. To learn more about distributed KV caching with ElastiCache and the performance benchmarks see the AWS blog. You can see getting started with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) at Amazon ElastiCache documentation and learn more about KVTrace at the GitHub repo.

General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. #7970. Latest Update: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1396 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • In a recent development, A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • Industry observers note that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

In a recent development, A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

Industry observers note that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That strategy is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Sources indicate that better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

According to recent reports, we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

Industry observers note that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

It has been revealed that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

Sources indicate that these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

Recent findings suggest that no single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

Industry observers note that A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That indicates nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It indicates how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

It has been revealed that gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Sources indicate that feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

In a recent development, out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

Industry observers note that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can blueprint around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

According to recent reports, the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together.
  • Industry observers note that AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work.
  • Sources indicate that AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together.

Industry observers note that AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done:.

Sources indicate that AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away.

It has been revealed that AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most key work. Now you can build, run, and refine flows entirely in chat. And your flows can take on more of your tough work, whether you start it from the web, desktop, or mobile app.

For example, here is how flows could support a finance team. Maya is a financial planning and analysis manager at a retailer. Each month, she prepares a report for her VP of Finance that explains changes to costs and margins. For each region, she pulls last month’s results, compares them to the plan in a spreadsheet, writes commentary on the biggest changes, and sends the report. The process lives in her memory and a personal checklist. When she is out, a teammate has to rebuild the report from scratch, and it looks different every time.

Industry observers note that with Quick, Maya can standardize the process, automate it, and make it available to her team. She describes her process in chat, the way she would explain it to a upcoming employee. Quick builds the flow from her description and she tests and refines it in the same conversation. A diagram beside the chat shows each step, so she can confirm it matches how she works.

Figure 1: Maya describes her monthly report in chat, and Quick builds the flow with a diagram beside it. Both views, enlarged here for visibility, appear side by side in the same Quick window.

A flow can now bring together agents, skills, tools, and data, and handle longer processes with more data. Fixed calculations and checks keep the results consistent, agents draft and analyze, and Maya decides what goes in the final report. On each run, her flow:.

Maya publishes the flow for her team. At the next month-end, she is at a planning meeting, so Jordan, an analyst on her team, runs it from chat in the Quick desktop app. There, the flow can use a spreadsheet of regional adjustments saved on his computer. Before the report goes out, Jordan reviews the draft, including why each region was flagged, asks for a few changes in chat, and approves it for the VP of Finance. When Priya joins the team, she runs the same flow at her first month-end, and the report is built the same way.

While this is a fictional example, real customers tell us they’re automating complex business processes to make them more consistent and repeatable. This gives their people back valuable time to focus on more strategic work. Take Pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider powering card issuance, processing, and payment operations for customers:.

Industry observers note that “At Pomelo, AWS Quick changed who gets to build solutions. Before, every analysis or automation depended on the data team. Today, people across every area explore information, make decisions, and build their own agents and flows within a unified, governed environment. Without growing our team, nearly four times as many people now work with data each month, so our data team can focus on its most complex, high-impact work. A single use case already saves us 80 hours of work per month. But the real transformation isn’t the hours we save. Quick is transforming our data and innovation culture: we’ve gone from a few people building solutions for many to an organization where everyone can create, experiment, and change the way they work. And we’re just getting started.”.

— Rodrigo Marini, Head of Data, Pomelo Fintech Services S.A.S.

If you already use Quick in your browser, the updated web app puts the items that need your attention on the home screen as soon as you sign in. A reorganized left navigation brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together under Customize. It includes the agents and skills you built on desktop and ones others have shared with you. Your existing dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before, and you do not need to turn anything on.

Figure 2: The feed brings the morning’s email and messages that need a reply into one view.

Industry observers note that some requests need the knowledge of more than one specialized agent. With multi-agent orchestration, the agent you ask can bring in several specialized agents at once, each working on the part it knows best. The agent then combines their work into one response. Each agent keeps its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so the people who know that work best can build and maintain it.

For example, you might ask why shipping costs rose in one region. Your agent can bring in a forecasting agent built on your team’s planning data and a procurement agent built on the procurement team’s vendor contracts. You get one response that reveals what each agent contributed, and you decide what to do with it.

Work lives in many systems. This release adds fresh connectors so Quick can pull from the analytics and tools your team uses every day. Connect once, then ask in natural language.

Meta ads. Create, manage, and analyze Meta ad campaigns in natural language through a connector to Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Quick combines Meta ad data with your first-party and third-party sources, and asks for your permission before it creates a campaign, changes a budget, or takes any other write action in an ad account. Try Quick free for 3 months and invite up to 10 teammates at no cost.

In a recent development, amplitude. Ask about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion in natural language. Quick connects to Amplitude through its MCP server, so product and marketing teams can pull behavioral insights into the dashboards, documents, and workflows they build in Quick.

Connectors respect your existing permissions. Quick only indicates each person what they already have access to. Quick asks before it takes any write action. Administrators choose which connectors teams can add.

Whether you build a monthly report, run one your manager built, or set up Quick for your organization, Quick works the way you do. Your data stays in your environment and does not train anyone else’s models. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals.

These features are available today in all Regions where AWS Quick is available.

In a recent development, to try what’s newly introduced, sign in to Quick or download Quick and get started in minutes. To learn about enterprise pricing looks, talk to your AWS account team.
